subtype: Approach: reading the timetable and packing the night before [Action]
passage:
Monday. Tanvir left packing for the morning, as always. At 7:40 he was still hunting for his Hindi notebook while the van honked, and he forgot his water bottle.
Tuesday evening. After dinner he took out the timetable taped inside his diary. Wednesday: English, Maths, Science, Art. He pulled out Tuesday's Hindi and Social Studies books, slid in the four he needed, then set his lunch box, washed and dry, and his bottle, filled and capped, by the door.
Wednesday morning. Tanvir ate his paratha slowly. His sister Charu, still hunting for her socks, stared at him. "Why are you so calm?" He pointed at his bag, zipped and waiting.

qa.q: Which subjects were on Wednesday's timetable?
qa.a: English, Maths, Science and Art.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel on Wednesday morning compared with Monday?
qa.a: On Monday he was rushed and flustered and forgot his bottle; on Wednesday he felt calm enough to eat his paratha slowly.

qa.q: What else could Tanvir add to his evening routine?
qa.a: A quick look through the diary for notes about projects or PT; packing in the evening is what freed up his morning.

qa.q: How does Charu see Tanvir's calm morning?
qa.a: Charu, still hunting for her socks, is surprised and a little puzzled by how calm he is.

grounding: Shows a boy reading tomorrow's timetable in the evening, swapping in the right books and setting out his lunch box and bottle, so the morning is calm.

subtype: Approach: reading the timetable and packing the night before [Action]
passage: Ojas, your bag looks like a storm hit it. Let your Deepika Atte tell you about your father. When Nikhil was in Class 4, every morning in our Mysuru house was a war: shouting for books, a missing tiffin, our mother running to the gate with his bottle. One evening our father sat him down with the timetable. 'Tomorrow, what's first?' Nikhil read it out: Kannada, Maths, EVS. He took out that day's books, put in tomorrow's, and set his tiffin box and bottle next to the bag. The next morning, for the first time, our mother drank her coffee sitting down. Nikhil kept that habit all the way to college.

qa.q: What subjects did Nikhil read out from the timetable?
qa.a: Kannada, Maths and EVS.

qa.q: How might young Nikhil have felt on that first calm morning?
qa.a: He was likely relieved and proud, with no shouting for books for the first time.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the mornings calm?
qa.a: Nikhil packing the night before from the timetable, so nothing had to be hunted for in the morning.

qa.q: What changed for their mother once Nikhil packed at night?
qa.a: She no longer had to run to the gate with his bottle; for the first time she drank her coffee sitting down.

grounding: Illustrates a boy packing the night before from the timetable, with tiffin and bottle ready, which turns rushed mornings calm.

subtype: Approach: using a coloured chart pinned on the wall [Action]
passage: In Class 6 I kept carrying the wrong books, so one Sunday I made a chart. I drew a big grid on chart paper: Monday to Saturday across the top, periods down the side. Then I gave each subject a colour: Maths blue, Science green, Hindi orange, English red. I coloured every box and pinned the chart on the wall right above my study table. That night, packing for Tuesday, I just looked for the colours: two blues, one green, one red. Done in a minute. My little brother Kashish said, 'Madhuri didi, it looks like a rainbow exploded.' Maybe. But I haven't carried a wrong book since.

qa.q: What colour did Madhuri give Maths?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel about packing once the chart was up?
qa.a: Madhuri felt relieved and pleased, since packing for Tuesday took only a minute of spotting colours 😊

qa.q: What could Madhuri do if a subject moves to a different day?
qa.a: Recolour that box or stick a note on it, so the chart stays true; the colours work because she can read a day at a glance.

qa.q: How does Kashish see the chart?
qa.a: Kashish teases that it looks like a rainbow exploded, so to him it seems funny and a bit much.

grounding: Shows a girl making a colour-coded weekly timetable chart by her study table so she can see which books belong to each day.

subtype: Approach: using a coloured chart pinned on the wall [Action]
passage: Class teacher's note, 7C, for the parents' meeting. Ayesha used to come without the right books two or three times a week. After the first term she showed me something she had made at home: a weekly chart where every subject had its own colour, pinned by her study table. She brought a photo of it. Now, she told me, she just matches colours when she packs. I've checked her bag on random days this month: every book right. Kashish, who sits beside her, has started a chart too, in felt pens. I'll suggest it to the whole class on Monday.

qa.q: How often did Ayesha use to come without the right books?
qa.a: Two or three times a week.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt showing the photo of her chart?
qa.a: She was probably proud and pleased to share something she made that fixed her problem.

qa.q: What could make the chart idea work for the whole class?
qa.a: Each student making a colour chart and pinning it where they pack, as Ayesha did, and updating it when the timetable changes.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Ayesha's chart?
qa.a: The note-writer checked her bag on random days, found every book right, and plans to suggest the idea to the class.

grounding: Illustrates a girl's colour-coded weekly chart by her study table helping her pack the right books, as seen by her teacher.

subtype: Approach: throwing everything in the bag just in case [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Vaibhav stuffed every book he owned into his bag. "Now I never have to check the timetable," he told his grandfather, Jagdish. The zip only just closed.
Wednesday. On the walk to school he kept shifting the bag from one shoulder to the other. By the gate there was a red line across his shoulder.
Friday. In the Science period, Ma'am asked for the lab notebook. Vaibhav dug through fourteen books, an atlas and a broken ruler. By the time he found it, the class had copied the diagram and moved on. That afternoon Dada Jagdish, waiting at the gate, carried the bag home, frowning at its weight.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav dig through in the Science period?
qa.a: Fourteen books, an atlas and a broken ruler.

qa.q: How was Vaibhav feeling on Friday as he dug through the bag?
qa.a: He was probably flustered and embarrassed, falling behind while the class moved on.

qa.q: What would you change first in Vaibhav's approach?
qa.a: Check the timetable each evening and pack only that day's books; carrying everything made the bag heavy and the notebook harder to find.

qa.q: How does Dada Jagdish see the bag?
qa.a: Dada Jagdish frowns at its weight as he carries it, so he seems worried about how heavy it is for Vaibhav.

grounding: Shows a boy carrying every book to avoid checking the timetable, until the bag hurts his shoulder and he still cannot find the right notebook.

subtype: Approach: throwing everything in the bag just in case [Pitfall]
passage: Kunal, why is your bag bulging like a pumpkin? Sit, and let your Mehak Nani tell you about your Mama, Sameer. When he was ten, he decided checking the timetable was a waste of time. So he carried everything: every book, every notebook, even his old drawing book. Every morning he went up the lane to school bent forward like an old man. His shoulders ached so badly he couldn't lift his arms to bowl in the evenings. And the funny part? One day his teacher asked for his English notebook, and he couldn't find it among twenty others. He got a remark in his diary for 'no homework'. And he had done it!

qa.q: What did Sameer's teacher ask for?
qa.a: His English notebook.

qa.q: How might young Sameer have felt when he got a remark for 'no homework'?
qa.a: He likely felt frustrated and unfairly treated, since he had actually done the homework but couldn't find it.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have saved Sameer his aching shoulders and the remark?
qa.a: Checking the timetable and packing only the day's books; carrying everything hurt his shoulders and buried the notebook.

qa.q: How might Sameer's teacher have seen the missing notebook?
qa.a: The teacher only saw homework that wasn't handed in, so it looked like none was done, though Sameer had done it.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who carries all his books to skip checking the timetable, ending up with aching shoulders and a notebook lost in the mess.

subtype: Approach: checking the bag against a short list at the door [Thinking]
passage: I stay with my cousin Payal's family, so I see her mornings. Taped inside the front door, at her eye level, is a list in her round handwriting: homework, diary, lunch, bottle, pencil box. Every morning, just before she steps out, she stops and taps each word, then touches the thing in her bag. Once I asked why she bothers. She said, 'When I'm in a hurry my brain says I packed it, and my brain lies.' Last week Tarun, her little brother, was yelling for his shoe and the van was honking. Payal still stopped. Tap, tap, tap. Bottle, missing. She ran back for it. I can't say whether she was nervous, but she didn't look it.

qa.q: Where is Payal's list taped?
qa.a: Inside the front door, at her eye level.

qa.q: Why does Payal tap each word even when the van is honking?
qa.a: She knows her memory 'lies' when she's in a hurry, so she seems determined and calm, trusting the list over the feeling of having packed.

qa.q: What else could Payal add to her list, and why?
qa.a: Things that change by day, like PT shoes, since the same check at the door would catch them.

qa.q: What might mornings be like for Tarun compared with Payal?
qa.a: Tarun is yelling for a shoe while the van honks, so his mornings seem much more rushed than Payal's calm tapping.

grounding: Shows a girl checking her bag against a five-item list at the door each morning because her memory is unreliable in a hurry.

subtype: Approach: checking the bag against a short list at the door [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Binita was sure she had packed her homework. In class it wasn't there. Elizabeth Ma'am wrote a note in her diary. "But I remember putting it in," Binita said, her face hot.
Tuesday. At home Binita sat and thought. When I'm rushing, I only think I remember. So she wrote a list on a card: homework, diary, lunch, bottle, pencil box. Five things. She stuck it on the door.
Thursday. The van horn blew. Binita stopped at the door and ticked the card, one, two, three... no diary. It was on the sofa. She grabbed it and ran. That afternoon, Elizabeth Ma'am's note went back signed.

qa.q: What was missing when Binita ticked the card on Thursday?
qa.a: Her diary; it was on the sofa.

qa.q: How did Binita feel on Monday when the homework wasn't there?
qa.a: Her face was hot, so she felt embarrassed and confused, sure she had packed it.

qa.q: Why does a written list work better than memory for Binita?
qa.a: She worked out that in a rush she only thinks she remembers; the card doesn't forget, so it caught the missing diary.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth Ma'am see the change by Thursday?
qa.a: After writing a note on Monday, Elizabeth Ma'am gets it back signed, which shows Binita is now keeping track.

grounding: Illustrates a girl realising her memory fails when she hurries and using a five-item list at the door to check her bag.

subtype: Approach: putting things back in the same place each day [Thinking]
passage:
"Eshaan, where's your geometry box? Maths is starting!"
"Front pocket." Eshaan pulled it out without looking.
"How did you do that? I've been hunting for my compass for five minutes."
"Last month I kept losing things too. So I thought, if the diary always lives in the back pocket and the geometry box always lives up front, I never have to think."
"Always?"
"Always. Even when I'm lazy. Especially when I'm lazy."
Dhruv unzipped his bag. Books, crumbs, a loose compass. "Mine lives... everywhere."
"Pick one place. Just for the compass. Start there."
The bell rang. Eshaan was already opening his box.

qa.q: Where does Eshaan keep his diary?
qa.a: In the back pocket.

qa.q: How does Eshaan seem to feel when the maths bell rings?
qa.a: He seems calm and relaxed, pulling out his box without looking while Dhruv is still hunting.

qa.q: What small step would help Dhruv start?
qa.a: Pick one fixed place just for the compass, as Eshaan suggests, and put it back there every time.

qa.q: How does Dhruv see Eshaan's habit?
qa.a: Dhruv is amazed, having hunted for his compass for five minutes, and begins to see that his own things live 'everywhere'.

grounding: Shows a boy explaining his rule that the geometry box always goes in the front pocket and the diary in the back, so he never has to search.

subtype: Approach: putting things back in the same place each day [Thinking]
passage: When I was in Class 5, the school bell was my enemy. It rang, and I'd be digging for my diary or my geometry box while everyone else was ready. One evening I sat on my bed and thought it through. The digging wasn't the real problem. The real problem was that my things lived in a different place every day. So I made a rule. Geometry box, front pocket. Diary, back pocket. Always, even when I'm tired. It felt silly for a week. Then one day the bell rang and my hand went to the front pocket without me thinking. My sister Jyoti noticed and said, 'Santosh bhai, since when are you so organised?'

qa.q: Where does Santosh keep his geometry box?
qa.a: In the front pocket.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel about the bell before his rule?
qa.a: Santosh called it an enemy, so he felt stressed and flustered, always digging while others were ready.

qa.q: What part of Santosh's thinking made the rule work?
qa.a: Seeing that the real problem was things living in different places, then keeping one place 'even when I'm tired' until it became automatic.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see the change?
qa.a: Jyoti is surprised and a little amused, asking since when Santosh became so organised.

grounding: Illustrates a boy reasoning that his things need fixed places, geometry box in front and diary at the back, so he need not think or search.

subtype: Approach: forgetting the change of timetable for PT day [Pitfall]
passage: Maria packed her bag on Tuesday night the way she had all term: Wednesday was maths, English, art. She didn't open her diary. The next morning at her Bengaluru school, the class lined up for PT, which had moved to Wednesday from this week. Everyone was in white canvas shoes except Maria, in her black school shoes. The PT sir shook his head. "No white shoes, no field." Maria sat on the steps by the ground with her chin on her knees, watching Jatin win the relay for their house. The notice about the change was folded in her diary, unread.

qa.q: Where was the notice about the change?
qa.a: Folded in her diary, unread.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling as she sat on the steps?
qa.a: Her chin on her knees suggests she felt left out and disappointed, missing the relay while others played.

qa.q: What would have prevented this?
qa.a: Checking the diary before packing on Tuesday night; packing from last week's memory missed the new PT day.

qa.q: How might Jatin see Maria sitting out?
qa.a: Jatin is busy with the relay, so Jatin may hardly notice, or may wonder why Maria is on the steps.

grounding: Shows a girl packing from last week's memory, missing the new Wednesday PT, and sitting out without white shoes.

subtype: Approach: forgetting the change of timetable for PT day [Pitfall]
passage:
"Vidya, where are your white shoes?"
"What white shoes?"
"It's Wednesday, Vidya. PT moved to Wednesday. It's been in the diary since Friday."
"No, PT is Thursday. It's always Thursday."
"It was Thursday. Sir changed it."
Vidya looked down at her black buckled shoes, then at the line of white ones. "I packed from memory. Like every week."
"Can you borrow some?"
"From who? Everyone's wearing theirs."
Sir blew his whistle. "Vidya, no white shoes? Sit on the bench, please."
From the bench Vidya watched Swati run the three-legged race with someone else. "I was supposed to be her partner," she muttered.

qa.q: What day did PT use to be on?
qa.a: Thursday.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel watching from the bench?
qa.a: She felt left out and disappointed, especially seeing Swati run with someone else when she was meant to be the partner.

qa.q: What small step would have saved Vidya's PT period?
qa.a: Reading the diary before packing instead of packing from memory; the change had been written there since Friday.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt about the race?
qa.a: Swati had to find a new partner at the last minute, so Swati may have felt sorry for Vidya and a bit let down.

grounding: Illustrates a girl who packs by memory of the old timetable, forgets PT has moved to Wednesday, and sits out without white shoes.

subtype: Approach: adding a note about changes to the plan [Revision]
passage: The week I missed PT because of my black shoes still stings a little. Sitting on that bench, I worked out what went wrong: my chart said nothing about PT, and I never looked at the diary. So that evening I wrote on a yellow sticky note, 'WEDNESDAY: PT SHOES!', and stuck it right on Wednesday's column. Then I made a Sunday rule: before dinner, I read the school diary for any change and fix the chart. Two Sundays later, the diary said library day had moved to Friday. I changed it. My little brother Samir laughed. 'Aditi didi, you're the timetable police.' Maybe. But I haven't sat on that bench since.

qa.q: What did Aditi write on the sticky note?
qa.a: 'WEDNESDAY: PT SHOES!'

qa.q: How does Aditi still feel about the missed PT week?
qa.a: It still stings a little, so Aditi felt embarrassed and left out, which pushed her to change the plan.

qa.q: What made Aditi's fix better than just trying to remember?
qa.a: The Sunday diary check catches new changes, like library day moving, and the note keeps them in front of her.

qa.q: How does Samir see Aditi's Sunday rule?
qa.a: Samir finds it funny and calls her the timetable police, even though it works.

grounding: Shows a girl who, after the PT shoe mistake, adds a sticky note for Wednesday PT to her chart and checks the diary every Sunday for changes.

subtype: Approach: adding a note about changes to the plan [Revision]
passage: Class teacher's note, 5B. Two weeks ago Rekha sat out PT for coming without white shoes; she had packed from the old timetable. I didn't scold her; she was upset enough. This week she showed me her timetable chart, now with a pink sticky note on Wednesday: 'PT shoes'. And now, she told me, she reads the school diary every Sunday evening with her mother and updates the chart. Ritu, her friend, has copied the sticky-note idea. Rekha has been on the field every Wednesday since. I've asked her to show her chart at Friday assembly.

qa.q: What colour was the sticky note on Wednesday?
qa.a: Pink.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel after sitting out PT?
qa.a: The note says she was upset enough, so she likely felt disappointed and embarrassed about missing PT.

qa.q: Why does Rekha's Sunday diary check matter as much as the sticky note?
qa.a: The note covers the change she already knows about, while the Sunday check catches the next change before it trips her up.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Rekha's fix?
qa.a: The note-writer is impressed enough to ask Rekha to show her chart at Friday assembly.

grounding: Illustrates a girl who, after missing PT, adds a sticky note for Wednesday PT shoes and checks the diary each Sunday for timetable changes.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent to pack it for him [Pitfall]
passage: Disha, you want Ammi to pack your bag every night? Let your Rehana Dadi tell you about your Abbu, Arif. When he was nine, I packed his bag every single night. He never once looked at the timetable. Then my cousin's wedding came, in Hyderabad, and I was away three days. The first morning, Arif packed alone. He put in Monday's books on a Thursday, because Monday was the only day he remembered. No science book, no English notebook. His teacher sent a note home with 'unprepared again' underlined twice. When I came back, he was waiting at the door, not to hug me, but to ask, 'Ammi, how do I read the timetable?'

qa.q: How long was Rehana away for the wedding?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: How might young Arif have felt when the teacher's note came home?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and helpless, having never learned to read the timetable himself.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have prevented Arif's trouble?
qa.a: Arif learning to pack from the timetable himself, with his Ammi checking at first, instead of her doing it every night.

qa.q: How did Arif's teacher see those days?
qa.a: The teacher only saw a boy arriving without the right books and underlined 'unprepared again', not knowing his mother usually packed for him.

grounding: Shows a boy who relied on his mother to pack his bag and, when she was away for a wedding, arrived with the wrong books.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent to pack it for him [Pitfall]
passage: Every night Rafiq's mother, Nirmala, packed his school bag while he watched cartoons. This week she had gone to a wedding in Pune, and on Tuesday night the power went out in a thunderstorm. Rafiq sat by a candle with his bag and the timetable, but the page looked like a code: periods, numbers, 'SST', 'EVS'. He'd never read it. He shoved in whatever looked familiar and went to bed. Wednesday at school: a Hindi book on a day with no Hindi, no maths notebook, and the drawing book for a class that was on Friday. Two teachers wrote in his diary. On the phone that evening, he asked his mother, very quietly, to teach him the timetable.

qa.q: What did Rafiq bring that he didn't need on Wednesday?
qa.a: A Hindi book on a day with no Hindi, and the drawing book for a class that was on Friday.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when he asked his mother on the phone?
qa.a: Asking 'very quietly' suggests he felt embarrassed and a little ashamed after two teachers wrote in his diary.

qa.q: What should change after this week?
qa.a: Nirmala could teach him to read the timetable and let him pack while she checks; relying on her left him lost when she was away.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see the phone call?
qa.a: Nirmala might feel sorry that her packing left him lost, and glad that he asked to learn.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who depends on his mother to pack his bag and, with her away at a wedding, takes the wrong books to school.

subtype: Approach: sorting loose papers into a folder each Friday [Action]
passage: Every Friday after school, Hana tipped her backpack upside down onto the living-room rug of their flat in Addis Ababa. Out fell pencil shavings, a squashed orange peel, crumpled spelling tests and notices. She sorted them into three piles: rubbish, worksheets to keep, notices for her parents. The rubbish went in the bin. Notices went to the fridge. Worksheets went into a blue plastic folder, newest at the front. Her brother Abebe watched from the sofa. "You do this every week?" "Every Friday." In September she had lost a trip form and missed the museum visit. Since October she hadn't lost a single paper.

qa.q: What were Hana's three piles?
qa.a: Rubbish, worksheets to keep, and notices for her parents.

qa.q: Why might Hana stick to this every Friday?
qa.a: She was disappointed to miss the museum visit after losing a trip form, and the routine helps her feel in control of her papers.

qa.q: What else could Hana add to her Friday routine?
qa.a: A quick look at next week's notices while sorting, so she knows about forms or dates coming up.

qa.q: How might Abebe see Hana's weekly sort?
qa.a: Abebe asks if she does it every week, so it may look like a lot of effort to him, even though it's working.

grounding: Shows a girl emptying her bag every Friday, binning scraps and filing worksheets and notices in a folder, so she loses fewer papers.

subtype: Approach: sorting loose papers into a folder each Friday [Action]
passage: Last period on Fridays in Class 6A was 'bag time', and most students spent it chatting. Gurleen used it. She emptied her bag onto her desk: a scrunched maths sheet, two notices about annual day, a sweet wrapper, a science worksheet with a tea stain. Wrapper and scraps into the class bin. Notices into the front pocket of her green plastic folder. Worksheets into the back, by subject. In the first term she had lost two forms; this term, none. Jagdish Sir, walking between the rows, stopped. 'Gurleen, did you get the annual day form?' She pulled it straight out of the folder. Half the class was still searching their bags.

qa.q: What colour is Gurleen's folder?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt pulling the form straight out?
qa.a: She was probably pleased and proud, while half the class was still searching 😊

qa.q: What would help the classmates who were still searching?
qa.a: Using Friday's bag time as Gurleen does: emptying the bag, binning scraps and filing notices in a folder.

qa.q: How does Jagdish Sir seem to see Gurleen's folder?
qa.a: Jagdish Sir asks her first and gets the form at once, so he likely sees her as reliable with papers.

grounding: Illustrates a girl clearing her bag each Friday and filing notices and worksheets in a folder, so over time she loses fewer papers.

subtype: Approach: making a guest list with a limit on numbers [Thinking]
passage: When I turned eleven, I wanted my whole class of thirty-eight at the party. Amma said our flat could fit fifteen, including cousins. That night I sat with a notebook and thought it through. First: who would I be sad without? Pema, obviously, and my cricket team, six of them. Then the cousins, four, because Amma said so and because I like them. Eleven. Then my bench partner, the two boys from tuition, and Kiran, who lent me his bat. Fifteen. Then I remembered Arvind. Sixteen. I sat for a long time. Arvind I only talk to at lunch. I crossed him out and felt a bit mean. Amma read the list and said, 'Harsha, my boy, that's a good list.'

qa.q: How many people could the flat fit?
qa.a: Fifteen, including cousins.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when he crossed Arvind out?
qa.a: Harsha felt a bit mean and torn, but decided a lunch-time classmate mattered less than those already on the list.

qa.q: What else could Harsha do for classmates he couldn't invite?
qa.a: Share sweets with the whole class at school so nobody feels completely left out; the list itself was fair because he started with who mattered most.

qa.q: How might Amma see Harsha's list?
qa.a: Amma sees he kept to fifteen and chose carefully, so she is pleased and calls it a good list.

grounding: Shows a boy limited to fifteen guests listing close friends and cousins first, counting, and cutting one to keep to the number.

subtype: Approach: making a guest list with a limit on numbers [Thinking]
passage: Note left for Ammu on the fridge, Saturday. While you were at work, Tanvir sat at the dining table for an hour with his party list. He wanted to ask all thirty of his class. I said fifteen is our limit; this flat can't hold more. He didn't argue. He wrote cousins first, five of them, then his closest friends, starting with Gurleen. He counted: seventeen. He looked at it a long time, then crossed out two boys from his van, saying, 'I only see them in the van.' He was quiet after that. I told him we'll send extra sweets for the van. Please look at his list tonight. Abbu

qa.q: How many names were on Tanvir's first count?
qa.a: Seventeen.

qa.q: How did Tanvir seem to feel after crossing out the two boys?
qa.a: He was quiet, which suggests he felt a bit sad or guilty about leaving them out.

qa.q: What else could help Tanvir feel better about the cut?
qa.a: Sending extra sweets for the van, as Abbu suggested, so the two boys still feel remembered.

qa.q: How does Abbu see the way Tanvir made the list?
qa.a: Abbu notices Tanvir accepted the limit without arguing and chose carefully, and wants Ammu to see the list too.

grounding: Illustrates a boy with a fifteen-guest limit listing cousins and close friends first, counting, and cutting two to fit.
